title: Basic Concepts and Atomic Structure
lines: This topic gives USAT many quick marks: mole calculations, Avogadro's number, molar volume, empirical formulas and limiting reactants; the gas laws and kinetic theory; types of solids and intermolecular forces; and atomic structure up to quantum numbers and electronic configurations. Arithmetic is light, so accuracy with formulas and molar masses decides the mark.
## The mole
One mole is the amount of substance containing Avogadro's number of particles, Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³.
| You know | Moles n =
| mass m (g) | m ÷ molar mass M
| number of particles N | N ÷ Nₐ
| volume of gas at STP | V ÷ 22.4 dm³
| solution | molarity × volume (dm³)
- STP means 0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm.
- Read the question: molecules, atoms or ions? One mole of H₂SO₄ contains 7 moles of atoms, including 4 of oxygen.
> Example 1. How many molecules and how many atoms are there in 4.4 g of CO₂ (C = 12, O = 16)?
> M = 44 g/mol, so n = 0.1 mol. Molecules = 0.1 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 6.02 × 10²². Each has 3 atoms, so atoms = 1.81 × 10²³.
## Formulas and stoichiometry
- Percentage of an element = (mass of that element in one formula ÷ molar mass) × 100.
- Empirical formula: divide each mass (or percentage) by the atomic mass, then divide by the smallest result to get a whole-number ratio.
- Molecular formula = n × empirical formula, where n = molar mass ÷ empirical formula mass. Glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ has the empirical formula CH₂O.
> Example 2. A compound contains 40.0 % carbon, 6.7 % hydrogen and 53.3 % oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula.
> C 40.0 ÷ 12 = 3.33; H 6.7 ÷ 1 = 6.7; O 53.3 ÷ 16 = 3.33. Dividing by 3.33 gives 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH₂O.
- Limiting reactant: divide the moles of each reactant by its coefficient in the balanced equation; the smallest result is the limiting reactant and fixes the amount of product.
- Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100.
> Example 3. 28 g of N₂ reacts with 4 g of H₂: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. Which is limiting, and what mass of NH₃ forms?
> N₂: 1 mol ÷ 1 = 1. H₂: 2 mol ÷ 3 = 0.67. H₂ is limiting. NH₃ formed = ⅔ × 2 mol = 4/3 mol = 4/3 × 17 ≈ 22.7 g.
## Gases
- Boyle: PV = constant at fixed T. Charles: V/T = constant at fixed P (T in kelvin). Combined: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
- Ideal gas equation PV = nRT, with R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ or 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.
- Avogadro: equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules.
- Dalton: total pressure = sum of partial pressures; each partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure.
- Graham: rate of diffusion ∝ 1/√M. Hydrogen diffuses four times as fast as oxygen. A gas that diffuses half as fast as O₂ has M = 4 × 32 = 128 g/mol.
- Kinetic theory: gas molecules move randomly and collide elastically; their average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature.
- Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour most at high pressure and low temperature. The van der Waals equation corrects for molecular attraction (a) and molecular volume (b).
## Liquids and solids
- Intermolecular forces, weakest to strongest for molecules of similar size: London (dispersion) forces < dipole-dipole forces < hydrogen bonds.
- Hydrogen bonding needs H joined to F, O or N. It explains why water is a liquid while H₂S is a gas, and why ice floats.
- A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, so water boils below 100 °C on a mountain and above it in a pressure cooker.
| Solid | Particles and forces | Example
| Ionic | ions, ionic bonds | NaCl, MgO
| Covalent network | atoms, covalent bonds | diamond, SiO₂
| Molecular | molecules, intermolecular forces | ice, iodine
| Metallic | cations in a sea of electrons | copper, iron
## Atomic structure
- Electron: discovered through cathode rays (J. J. Thomson); mass 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Proton: from positive rays. Neutron: discovered by Chadwick (1932).
- Rutherford's α-scattering showed that an atom is mostly empty space with a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
- Atomic number Z = protons; mass number A = protons + neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z and different numbers of neutrons.
- Bohr: the electron in hydrogen occupies fixed orbits; energy is emitted or absorbed only when it jumps between them.
- Quantum numbers: n (shell, 1, 2, 3 …), l (subshell, 0 to n − 1: s, p, d, f), m (orientation, −l to +l) and s (spin, ±½).
- A shell holds 2n² electrons; subshells hold s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14.
## Filling orbitals
- Aufbau: fill in order of increasing (n + l); for equal (n + l), lower n first. Order: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s.
- Pauli: no two electrons have the same four quantum numbers, so an orbital holds at most two, with opposite spins.
- Hund: electrons enter degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing.
- Exceptions: Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, because half-filled and filled d subshells are extra stable.
> Example 4. How many unpaired electrons do Cr and Fe²⁺ have?
> Cr is 3d⁵ 4s¹: all six electrons are unpaired. Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; Fe²⁺ loses the 4s electrons first, leaving 3d⁶ with 4 unpaired.
! The reactant with fewer moles is not always limiting; compare moles divided by coefficients.
! Use kelvin in all gas-law work: heating from 27 °C to 127 °C raises V by 400/300, not by 127/27.
! There is no 2d or 1p orbital: l can only run from 0 to n − 1.
## Quick check
- Volume of 0.5 mol of a gas at STP? (11.2 dm³)
- Moles of ions from one mole of CaCl₂? (3)
- Maximum electrons in the n = 3 shell? (18)
- Which fills first, 4s or 3d? (4s)
- Which gas diffuses faster, NH₃ or HCl? (NH₃, lower molar mass)
